title: Linux Essentials (010-200) practice exam

domains.name: The Linux Operating System and Open Source Software

note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from LPI's public Linux Essentials 010-200 objectives, version 2.0 only (https://www.lpi.org/our-certifications/exam-010-objectives/, checked 2026-11-26). Not real exam questions. The real exam has 40 questions in 60 minutes; this bank has a larger pool and 3 hands-on items, and draws an exam by the official topic weights (18, 22, 22, 20 and 18 percent).

q.title: Find out why a service will not start
q.scenario: On your own practice VM, the notes web service stopped after an update. You have written approval from the VM's owner (you) and sudo rights on this machine only. Find out why it failed, fix it with the least access needed, and start it again. Do not wipe logs or open files to everyone.
q.ticket: Lab ticket LE-210: service notes is down on labvm. Scope: this VM only. The service runs as the system user notes. The config file holds a database password.
q.intro: labvm (Ubuntu practice VM, user student, sudo allowed). Type a command.

cmds.out:
x notes.service - Notes web service
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/notes.service; enabled)
     Active: failed (Result: exit-code) since Wed 2026-11-25 16:05:02 UTC; 3min ago
    Process: 2210 ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/notes (code=exited, status=1/FAILURE)

alt.out:
* notes.service - Notes web service
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/notes.service; enabled)
     Active: active (running) since Wed 2026-11-25 16:09:41 UTC; 5s ago

cmds.out:
Nov 25 16:05:02 labvm systemd[1]: Started Notes web service.
Nov 25 16:05:02 labvm notes[2210]: FATAL: cannot open /etc/notes/app.conf: Permission denied
Nov 25 16:05:02 labvm systemd[1]: notes.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
Nov 25 16:05:02 labvm systemd[1]: notes.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'.

Job for notes.service failed because the control process exited with error code.
See "systemctl status notes.service" and "journalctl -xeu notes.service" for details.
Not run. The file holds a database password, and this would let every account on the machine read it. Give the notes service access, not everyone.
Not run. This destroys logs or the configuration you are trying to fix. Look first, then make the smallest change.

checks.t: Checked the service state with systemctl
checks.why: systemctl status shows the service is failed and that its start command exited with an error. It is the first stop for any service problem.

checks.t: Read the service's log with journalctl
checks.why: journalctl -u notes shows the exact reason: the service could not open /etc/notes/app.conf because of Permission denied.

checks.t: Looked at the file's owner and permissions with ls -l
checks.why: ls -l shows the file belongs to root and group root, with no permissions for others. The notes user falls in the 'others' part, so it cannot read it.

checks.t: Fixed it by giving the notes group the file
checks.why: Making notes the group lets the existing rw-r----- mode give the service read access, and everyone else stays locked out. That is the least access that works.

checks.t: Restarted the service after the fix
checks.why: The service only reads its config at start. Restarting after the fix brings it up, while a restart before the fix would fail again.

checks.t: Did not open the file to everyone or wipe logs and config
checks.why: chmod 777 or 644 would expose a database password to every account, and deleting logs or the config removes the evidence you need. Smallest safe change first.

q.title: Read the login log of a Linux server
q.scenario: srv1 is a lab Linux server that you run for practice. You have written approval to review its authentication log. Mark every line that belongs to an attack, then say what happened and what to do first.
q.ticket: Lab ticket LE-215: weekly review of /var/log/auth.log on srv1. Scope: reading this log only.

lines.text: Nov 25 03:00:01 srv1 CRON[2201]: pam_unix(cron:session): session opened for user root by (uid=0)
lines.why: The nightly cron job runs at 03:00 as root. A scheduled session at a set time is routine.

lines.text: Nov 25 08:02:11 srv1 sshd[3140]: Accepted publickey for amy from 10.0.4.22 port 50122 ssh2
lines.why: Amy signs in with her key from an inside address, the way she normally does.

lines.text: Nov 25 09:14:40 srv1 sshd[3392]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.9 port 40001 ssh2
lines.why: A password try for an account that does not exist, from an outside address. This starts a guessing run.

lines.text: Nov 25 09:14:42 srv1 sshd[3394]: Failed password for invalid user test from 203.0.113.9 port 40003 ssh2
lines.why: The same address now tries another common name two seconds later. Guessing, not a user who forgot something.

lines.text: Nov 25 09:14:45 srv1 sshd[3397]: Failed password for invalid user oracle from 203.0.113.9 port 40006 ssh2
lines.why: A third made-up name from the same address in five seconds is a scripted attack.

lines.text: Nov 25 09:14:49 srv1 sshd[3401]: Failed password for amy from 203.0.113.9 port 40009 ssh2
lines.why: The attacker now tries a real account name. Amy normally logs in from an inside address, not this one.

lines.text: Nov 25 09:14:53 srv1 sshd[3405]: Accepted password for amy from 203.0.113.9 port 40012 ssh2
lines.why: A password login for Amy from the outside address, after failures. She uses keys. The guess worked.

lines.text: Nov 25 09:15:30 srv1 sudo: amy : TTY=pts/1 ; PWD=/home/amy ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/sbin/useradd -m support
lines.why: Right after the login, an account called support is created with root rights. That is an attacker setting up a way back in.

lines.text: Nov 25 09:16:02 srv1 sudo: amy : TTY=pts/1 ; PWD=/home/amy ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/tee -a /root/.ssh/authorized_keys
lines.why: Adding a key to root's authorized_keys gives lasting root login that survives a password change.

lines.text: Nov 25 09:40:15 srv1 sshd[3480]: Accepted publickey for bob from 10.0.4.30 port 51200 ssh2
lines.why: Bob uses a key from an inside address. Nothing odd.

lines.text: Nov 25 10:05:12 srv1 sshd[3511]: Failed password for bob from 10.0.4.30 port 51244 ssh2
lines.why: One failed password from an inside address is a typing mistake. It is not a pattern.

lines.text: Nov 25 10:05:18 srv1 sshd[3512]: Accepted password for bob from 10.0.4.30 port 51250 ssh2
lines.why: Bob succeeded on his next try from the same address. Normal.

ask.label: What does this log show, and what is the best first step?
opts: An outside address guessed Amy's password, then added a user and a root key; block it and remove them
A normal morning with a few mistyped passwords, so nobody needs to do anything about it
A broken cron job that runs at the wrong time, so edit the crontab and set a new schedule
A system update that created a new user account, so restart the server to finish it
ask.why: The outside address tried several names, got Amy's password, then used sudo to create the support account and plant a root key. Stop the access and remove what was added. The mistyped password is Bob's inside login and is harmless. No cron fault or update creates these steps.

q.title: Set up a team folder with the right permissions
q.scenario: On a practice Linux server you own, a small team needs a shared folder at /srv/ops. Members of the group ops must read and write there, and nobody else may enter. Add the steps in a sensible order. Some ideas do not belong.
q.ticket: Lab ticket LE-220: create the shared folder /srv/ops for group ops. You are the administrator of this practice server.

rules.text: Create the group ops with groupadd
rules.why: The group must exist before you can give it a folder or add people to it.

rules.text: Add the team members to the group ops
rules.why: With the group in place, members are added so they get access.
The folder must exist before you can change its group or permissions.

rules.text: Set the folder's group to ops with chgrp
rules.why: This ties the folder to the group. It needs both the group and the folder to exist.

rules.text: Set the mode to 770 with chmod
rules.why: Owner and group get full access, and others get none.
Checking last proves the owner, group and mode are what you intended.

rules.text: Set the mode to 777 so nothing can go wrong
rules.why: 777 lets every user read, change and delete files in the folder. It defeats the point of a team folder.

rules.text: Give every team member full sudo rights
rules.why: Folder access needs a group, not root rights. Extra sudo access is more power than anyone needs.

rules.text: Copy the team's passwords into a shared file
rules.why: Sharing passwords breaks accountability and is never needed to share a folder.

before.why: A user can only be added to a group that exists.
The group has to exist before it can be set on the folder.
The folder has to exist before you can change its group.
Set the group first, then the mode, so the group bits apply to the right group.

last.why: A final listing proves the result before the team starts to use the folder.

q.q: In a Linux system, which part is the kernel?
o: The desktop and the apps that sit on top
The desktop, tools and apps are userspace. They ask the kernel to do the low-level work.
The installer image used to set up a PC
An installer image is only the media used to put the system on a disk. It is not a running part of the system.
The online store that holds software packages
That is a package repository. It supplies software but does not control the hardware.
The core that manages hardware, memory and running programs
Right. The kernel sits between programs and the hardware. Everything else is built on top of it.

q.q: A unit wants a server that gets security fixes for several years without big feature changes. Which release type fits best?
o: A rolling release that updates continuously
A rolling release keeps pulling in new versions. That means frequent change, which is the opposite of what the unit asked for.
A long-term support (LTS) release
Right. LTS releases promise fixes for a long, fixed period and keep changes small, which suits servers.
A nightly build for developers
Nightly builds are unfinished test versions. They are not meant for production servers.
A beta image built for testers
A beta is a preview. It has no long support promise.

q.q: How does Android relate to Linux?
o: It uses the Linux kernel with its own user-facing software on top
Right. Android runs on a modified Linux kernel, but its apps, libraries and interface are Google's own, so it is not a classic distribution.
It is a Debian spin that installs software with apt
Android does not use apt or Debian packages. Its apps come as APK files.
It has its own kernel with no Linux code
Android's kernel is Linux-based, so this is wrong.
It is a Windows layer made to run phone apps
Android is not built on Windows in any way.

q.q: A container image must stay very small and starts from a distribution that uses the apk package tool. Which distribution is that?
o: Ubuntu Server
Ubuntu belongs to the Debian family and installs packages with apt.
Rocky Linux
Rocky is an Enterprise Linux system and uses dnf.
Alpine Linux
Right. Alpine is tiny and uses apk, which is why it is popular as a base for containers.
openSUSE
openSUSE belongs to the SUSE family and uses zypper.

q.q: Windows laptops need to open shared folders that live on a Linux file server. Which software provides that sharing?
o: NGINX
NGINX serves web pages and acts as a proxy. It does not share folders with Windows.
Samba
Right. Samba speaks the file-sharing protocol that Windows uses, so Windows clients can reach Linux shares.
PostgreSQL
PostgreSQL is a database server. It stores tables, not shared folders.
LibreOffice
LibreOffice is an office suite for documents and spreadsheets.

q.q: Which command installs the package nginx on a Rocky Linux server?
o: apt install nginx
apt belongs to Debian and Ubuntu systems.
zypper install nginx
zypper is the package tool of the SUSE family.
dnf install nginx
Right. Rocky Linux is an Enterprise Linux system, and dnf is its package tool.
apk add nginx
apk is the package tool of Alpine Linux.

q.q: The Linux kernel itself is mostly written in which language?
o: Python
Python is a popular scripting language, but the kernel is not written in it.
JavaScript
JavaScript mostly runs in web browsers. It is not used to build the kernel.
PHP
PHP is a web scripting language and is not used for kernels.
C
Right. C is compiled into fast machine code and lets the kernel work close to the hardware.

q.q: A developer wants anyone who shares changed copies of the code to share them under the same terms. Which kind of license does that?
o: A copyleft license such as the GPL
Right. Copyleft means changes must stay under the same free terms when shared.
A permissive license such as BSD
Permissive licenses let others reuse the code, even in closed products, with few rules.
A Creative Commons license
Creative Commons licenses are for creative works like photos and text, not mainly for software.
A closed-source user agreement
That keeps the code private. It does not require sharing changes.

q.q: Which group maintains the Open Source Definition and approves licenses against it?
o: Creative Commons
Creative Commons writes licenses for creative works. It does not maintain the Open Source Definition.
The Open Source Initiative (OSI)
Right. OSI keeps the Open Source Definition and lists licenses that meet it.
The Linux Professional Institute
LPI runs Linux certifications. It does not approve licenses.
The Wi-Fi Alliance
That group certifies wireless gear. It has nothing to do with software licenses.

q.q: A unit wants to publish its training photos so that others may reuse them if they give credit. Which license family was made for this?
o: Creative Commons
Right. Creative Commons licenses are made for sharing photos, text and other creative works, and one option only asks for credit.
GNU General Public License
The GPL is aimed at software source code.
BSD license
The BSD license is a permissive software license.
A hardware warranty
A warranty is a promise about repairs. It is not a license for reuse.

q.q: Which statement about where Linux is used is true?
o: It runs mostly on desktop computers and few servers
Desktops are only a small share. Servers and embedded devices are far more common.
It runs in a virtual machine only with special licenses
Linux runs in virtual machines freely and is very common there.
It needs a graphical desktop for most server jobs
Most servers run with no graphical desktop at all.
It runs on cloud servers, embedded devices and phones
Right. Linux is used across many device types, from tiny embedded boards to large cloud server farms.

q.q: You are in vi and have pressed Esc. Which keys save the file and quit?
o: :q! then Enter
This quits and throws away your changes.
Ctrl+X
That is the quit key in nano. In vi it does nothing useful here.
:wq then Enter
Right. In vi, :w writes the file and :q quits, so :wq does both.
i then Enter
The i key switches to insert mode so you can type. It does not save.

q.q: A website offers a passkey sign-in. What is a main benefit over a typed password?
o: It is a short code you may reuse on several trusted sites
Passkeys are tied to one site each. They are not reusable codes.
It sends your password in clear text faster
A passkey is not a password and nothing is sent in clear text.
It turns off HTTPS to save time
HTTPS stays on. A passkey does not replace it.
A secret key stays on your device, so there is nothing to type or phish
Right. Passkeys use a private key held on the device. A fake site can't trick you into typing it.

q.q: You find an unknown USB drive in the parking lot. What is the safest action?
o: Plug it into a lab PC to see what is on it
That risks infecting the PC. Even a lab PC can be on the network.
Plug it into your phone to scan it
A phone is not a safe test box, and it may hold work data.
Do not plug it in and hand it to your security office
Right. Unknown drives can carry malware or act like a keyboard that types commands. Report it instead of testing it.
Format it on your laptop and reuse it
Even connecting it to a laptop is the risk you are trying to avoid.

q.q: A user named kim runs: echo 'Hi $USER'. What does it print?
o: Hi $USER
Right. Single quotes stop the shell from expanding variables, so the text is printed exactly as typed.
Hi kim
That would happen with double quotes. Single quotes block the expansion.
Hi
That would only happen if the variable were empty and expanded.
An error about the quote
The command is valid. Quoted text is fine.

q.q: You set PROJ=alpha in your shell. A script you run from it cannot see PROJ. Which command makes the variable available to the script?
o: unset PROJ
unset removes the variable completely.
export PROJ
Right. export marks the variable so child processes, like a script, inherit it.
alias PROJ
alias makes a command shortcut. It does not pass variables on.
history PROJ
history lists past commands. It does not change variables.

q.q: Running type cd shows that cd is a shell builtin. What does that mean?
o: It is a program stored in /usr/bin
type would then show a file path instead of builtin.
It is a shortcut the user made
A shortcut would be reported as an alias.
It is part of bash itself and has no separate program file
Right. Builtins run inside the shell. That is why cd can change the shell's own directory.
It can only be used by the root user
Any user can run cd. Builtin has nothing to do with privilege.

q.q: A script named tool sits in your current folder. Typing tool says command not found, but ./tool works. What is the most likely reason?
o: The current directory is not listed in PATH
Right. The shell only searches the folders in PATH. The ./ prefix points straight at the file.
The file name is too short
Length of the name does not matter.
The shell is in read-only mode
There is no such mode that blocks commands by name.
The script was written in uppercase
The file name case would only matter if you typed it differently.

q.q: Which command opens the manual page that explains the file format of /etc/passwd (manual section 5)?
o: passwd --help
That prints short usage for the passwd command, not the file format.
man 5 passwd
Right. man takes the section number first. Section 5 covers file formats.
help passwd
help covers shell builtins. passwd is a program.
whatis passwd
whatis shows a one-line summary only.

q.q: Which command prints a short usage summary straight to the terminal, without opening the full manual?
o: man cp
This opens the full manual in a pager.
whatis cp
This prints one line describing the command.
type cp
This only tells you how the shell interprets the name.
cp --help
Right. Most GNU tools accept --help and print a quick summary.

q.q: Where do many installed packages keep extra documentation such as README files and examples?
o: /usr/local/readme
/etc holds configuration files, not documentation.
/var/spool
/var/spool holds queued work such as print jobs.
/usr/share/doc
Right. Packages place docs in a folder under /usr/share/doc.
/boot
/boot holds the kernel and boot loader files.

q.q: Which option makes ls also show hidden files, such as .bashrc?
o: ls -l
-l gives the long format but still hides dot files.
ls -h
-h only makes sizes readable, and only along with -l.
ls -t
-t sorts by time. It does not change which files appear.
ls -a
Right. The -a option means all, so names that start with a dot are shown too.

q.q: Your current folder is /home/ana/docs. Which relative path reaches /home/ana/pics?
o: ../pics
Right. The two dots mean the parent folder (/home/ana), and pics is inside it.
./pics
./ means the current folder, which would be /home/ana/docs/pics.
../../pics
That climbs two levels to /home, giving /home/pics.
/pics
The leading slash makes it absolute, starting at the top of the tree.

q.q: In bash, what does the ~ symbol stand for?
o: The top folder of the whole file system
The top is / and is called the root directory.
The home folder of the current user
Right. The shell expands ~ to the home directory, such as /home/ana.
The folder you were in before
That is what cd - uses, not the tilde.
The parent of the current folder
The parent folder is written ..

q.q: Which command finds a file named report.txt anywhere under /srv?
o: find report.txt /srv
find expects the folder first. The name would be read as a start folder.
find /srv -name report.txt
Right. find takes the starting folder first, then the test, here -name.
find /srv -type report.txt
-type takes f, d and similar letters, not a file name.
find -name /srv report.txt
The options are in the wrong places and the command would fail.

q.q: A folder holds both Report.txt and report.txt. Why is that possible?
o: One of them is a hidden copy
Hidden files start with a dot. These do not.
One is a link the other cannot change
Neither is a link just because the case differs.
The system will soon delete one
Nothing is removed. Both names stay.
Linux file names are case sensitive, so they are two files
Right. Upper and lower case letters make different names on a Linux file system.

q.q: Which command deletes only the files ending in .log in the current folder?
o: rm .log
This would try to remove a single file named .log.
rm log.*
This matches names starting with log. and may hit other files.
rm *.log
Right. The * wildcard matches any name, and .log limits it to names ending that way.
rm -r *
This deletes everything in the folder, including folders.

q.q: Which command renames draft.txt to final.txt?
o: mv draft.txt final.txt
Right. mv moves a file, and moving to a new name in the same folder is a rename.
cp draft.txt final.txt
cp keeps the old file and makes a copy.
touch draft.txt final.txt
touch creates or updates files. It does not rename.
mkdir draft.txt final.txt
mkdir creates folders.

q.q: You need the nested folders a/b/c, but a does not exist yet. Which single command creates them?
o: mkdir a/b/c
Without -p this fails because a/b does not exist.
rmdir a/b/c
rmdir removes empty folders. It does not create them.
mkdir a ; mkdir b ; mkdir c
This makes three separate folders side by side in the current folder, not a nested chain.
mkdir -p a/b/c
Right. The -p option creates every missing parent folder along the way.

q.q: Which command creates a gzip-compressed archive named docs.tar.gz from the folder docs?
o: tar -czf docs.tar.gz docs
Right. c creates, z compresses with gzip and f names the file.
tar -xzf docs.tar.gz docs
x extracts, so this unpacks an archive instead of making one.
tar -tzf docs.tar.gz docs
t lists the contents of an existing archive.
gunzip docs.tar.gz docs
gunzip undoes gzip compression. It does not create anything.

q.q: How can you list what is inside backup.tar without extracting it?
o: tar -xf backup.tar
x extracts the files into the current folder.
tar -cf backup.tar
c creates an archive and could overwrite the one you have.
tar -tf backup.tar
Right. The t option lists the contents and leaves the files alone.
tar -zf backup.tar
z handles gzip and still needs an action letter like t or x.

q.q: Of gzip, bzip2 and xz, which usually makes the smallest file but takes the longest?
o: gzip
gzip is the fastest of the three but makes larger files.
xz
Right. xz trades speed for a better compression ratio.
bzip2
bzip2 sits in the middle for both speed and size.
tar
tar bundles files but does not compress by itself.

q.q: What does the command ls /etc | wc -l print?
o: The total size of /etc in bytes
wc -l counts lines, not bytes, and ls does not print a size total here.
The number of names listed in /etc
Right. The pipe sends the list to wc, and -l counts its lines.
The word count of every file in /etc
The pipe carries the names, not the file contents.
Nothing, because a pipe needs a file
A pipe connects the output of one command to the next without a file.

q.q: You want to add the line done to the end of log.txt without erasing what is there. Which command does it?
o: echo done > log.txt
A single > overwrites the whole file.
echo done < log.txt
< feeds a file into a command as input.
echo done >> log.txt
Right. >> appends to the file.
echo done | tee log.txt
tee without -a overwrites the file, so the old lines would be lost.

q.q: Which command line uses the second output stream, to send only error messages to errors.txt?
o: backup.sh 2> errors.txt
Right. File number 2 is standard error, so 2> sends just the errors to the file.
backup.sh > errors.txt
This sends normal output, not the errors, to the file.
backup.sh < errors.txt
This reads the file as input.
backup.sh | tee errors.txt
tee copies normal output to the file. Error messages are not sent through the pipe.

q.q: Why do you usually run sort before uniq?
o: uniq can only read sorted files stored in /etc
uniq has no such folder limit.
sort deletes blank lines that break uniq
sort does not delete lines.
uniq refuses to run on text files
uniq works on text. The problem is only about neighbors.
uniq only merges duplicate lines that are next to each other
Right. Sorting puts equal lines side by side so uniq can merge or count them.

q.q: A text file uses colons between its fields. Which command prints only the first field of every line of /etc/passwd?
o: cut -d' ' -f1 /etc/passwd
This splits on spaces, but the fields are separated by colons, so each whole line prints.
cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd
Right. -d sets the delimiter to a colon and -f1 picks the first field.
cut -c1 /etc/passwd
-c1 prints only the first character of each line.
grep -f1 /etc/passwd
-f in grep reads patterns from a file, so this is wrong.

q.q: Which command shows lines in app.log that contain either error or fail?
o: grep 'error|fail' app.log
Without -E, GNU grep takes the bar as a plain character.
grep -v 'error|fail' app.log
-v would show the lines that do not match.
grep -c error fail app.log
This treats fail as a file name, and -c only counts.
grep -E 'error|fail' app.log
Right. With -E, the bar means or, so either word matches.

q.q: A script runs with bash deploy.sh but ./deploy.sh says Permission denied. What is the best fix?
o: chown root deploy.sh
Changing the owner does not add execute permission.
export deploy.sh
export is for variables, not for permissions.
chmod +x deploy.sh
Right. Running a file directly needs the execute permission, and chmod +x adds it.
mv deploy.sh /bin
Moving the file is not needed and may also need extra rights.

q.q: Inside a bash script, which variable holds the first argument given on the command line?
o: Right. $1 is the first argument, $2 the second, and so on.
$0 holds the name of the script itself.
$# holds how many arguments were given.
$? holds the exit status of the last command.

q.q: Right after a command finishes, which command shows its exit status?
o: echo $$
$$ is the process number of the current shell.
echo $!
$! is the process number of the last background job.
echo $0
$0 is the name of the script or shell.
echo $?
Right. $? holds the exit status of the last command. Zero means success.

q.q: Which test is true when /etc/hosts exists and is a regular file?
o: [ -f /etc/hosts ]
Right. -f checks for a regular file.
[ -d /etc/hosts ]
-d checks for a directory.
[ -z /etc/hosts ]
-z checks whether a string is empty.
[ -x /etc/hosts ]
-x checks the execute permission, not whether the file exists.

q.q: What does for f in *.txt; do echo "$f"; done print?
o: The contents of each .txt file
echo prints the name held in the variable, not the file's text.
The name of each .txt file in the folder, one per line
Right. The loop runs once for every name that the wildcard matches.
Only the first .txt file name
The loop goes through every match.
Nothing, because for needs a number range
for can loop over any list of words, including a wildcard.

q.q: Which feature lets a Windows PC run a Linux command-line environment without rebooting?
o: A dual-boot setup
Dual boot needs a restart to switch between systems.
A Live ISO on USB
A live USB boots Linux in place of Windows.
Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL)
Right. WSL runs Linux tools alongside Windows apps on the same machine.
A BIOS update
A BIOS update changes firmware and does not run Linux.

q.q: A cloud provider lets you start a ready-made Linux server in minutes from a stored template. What is the server called?
o: A dual-boot partition
Dual boot uses the disk of one local computer.
A kernel module
A module adds a driver to a running kernel.
A bootloader entry
A bootloader entry only lists a system to start.
An instance created from an image
Right. A cloud instance is a virtual server that starts from an image.

q.q: What happens to data you write to /dev/null?
o: It is saved to the first disk
The first disk is a different device, such as /dev/sda.
It is discarded and never stored
Right. /dev/null is a special device that swallows everything written to it.
It becomes a stream of random bytes
Random bytes come out of /dev/urandom, not /dev/null.
It is sent to the printer
Printers are not handled by this device.

q.q: What does the device name /dev/sda1 normally refer to?
o: The second disk in the machine, whatever its type
The second disk would be /dev/sdb.
The first network card
Network cards do not appear as device files in /dev this way.
The first partition of the first sd disk
Right. sda is the first SATA, SCSI-style or USB disk, and the number 1 is its first partition.
The first CPU core
CPU cores are not shown as files like this.

q.q: Which command lists the kernel modules that are currently loaded?
o: lsmod
Right. lsmod prints the loaded modules, which are drivers and other kernel add-ons.
lspci
lspci lists devices on the PCI bus.
lsblk
lsblk lists disks and partitions.
lscpu
lscpu shows information about the processor.

q.q: Which command gives a live view of running processes, refreshed every few seconds?
o: free
free shows memory totals, not processes.
uptime
uptime shows how long the system has run and the load average.
ps aux
ps prints one snapshot and exits, rather than refreshing.
top
Right. top updates its list of processes and their CPU and memory use as you watch.

q.q: Which command starts the sshd service now and also makes it start at every boot?
o: systemctl start sshd
start runs it now only. It will not return after a reboot.
systemctl enable sshd.service
enable alone sets the boot behavior and does not start it now.
systemctl enable --now sshd
Right. enable sets it to start at boot, and --now also starts it immediately.
systemctl status sshd
status only shows its current state.

q.q: Which command shows the log lines for the nginx service since the system last booted?
o: journalctl -u nginx -b
Right. -u picks the unit and -b limits output to the current boot.
dmesg nginx
dmesg shows kernel messages and takes no service name.
cat /proc/nginx
/proc has no file with that name.
systemctl journal nginx --boot
systemctl has no log command.

q.q: A USB device was plugged in and you want the kernel's own messages about it. Which command shows them?
o: free -h
free reports memory use.
dmesg
Right. dmesg prints the kernel's message buffer, which includes hardware events.
ps aux
ps lists processes.
uptime
uptime shows how long the system has run.

q.q: Which command shows the IP addresses assigned to this computer's network interfaces?
o: ip route
ip route lists the routes and the default gateway.
ip addr
Right. ip addr lists every interface and the addresses it holds.
ss -tln
ss lists sockets, such as listening ports.
ping localhost
ping tests whether a host answers. It does not list addresses.

q.q: Which command shows the default gateway your computer uses?
o: ip addr
ip addr shows addresses on interfaces, not routes.
resolvectl status
This shows DNS settings, not the gateway.
ss -s
This prints socket statistics.
ip route
Right. The route table has a default entry that names the gateway.

q.q: A technician wants to point a name at a fixed IP address on one computer only, without using DNS. Which file is checked for that?
o: /etc/hosts
Right. The hosts file maps names to addresses locally and is usually checked first.
/etc/resolv.conf
This lists the DNS servers to ask.
/etc/shadow
This stores password hashes.
/etc/skel
This holds starter files for new home folders.

q.q: An IPv6 laptop builds its own address from router announcements and no server keeps a lease list. What is this called?
o: DHCPv6
DHCPv6 can hand out addresses from a server that keeps a lease list.
NAT
NAT rewrites addresses on a router. It does not create host addresses.
SLAAC
Right. Stateless address autoconfiguration lets the host form its own IPv6 address.
ARP
ARP finds the hardware address that matches an IPv4 address on the local network.

q.q: Which command lists TCP ports where a service is listening on this computer?
o: ip link
ip link shows the network interfaces and their state.
ss -tln
Right. ss shows sockets, and -t -l -n limits it to listening TCP sockets with numbers.
host example.org
host looks up a DNS name.
ping -c1 example.org
ping tests if one remote host answers.

q.q: Why do admins often run single commands with sudo instead of logging in as root?
o: It means your own password is checked less often than usual
sudo normally asks for your password, and it does not relax that check.
It turns your account into a system account
Your account type does not change.
It lets that command skip some file permission checks
Root already ignores most permission checks. sudo does not switch permissions off.
Only that command runs with root rights, and it is logged
Right. sudo limits the time spent as root and leaves a record of who did what.

q.q: On the server, which file lists the public keys allowed to log in to a user's account?
o: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
This is your own public key file on the client. It is not the list of keys the server allows.
~/.ssh/known_hosts
This is the client's list of server fingerprints.
~/.ssh/authorized_keys
Right. The server reads this file in the user's home folder to match the key a client offers.
/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key
This is the server's own private host key. It proves the server's identity and lists nobody.

q.q: Which command copies report.pdf to /srv/in on the host fs1 as the user ana?
o: scp report.pdf ana@fs1:/srv/in
Right. scp uses source first, then user@host:path for the remote end.
scp ana@fs1 report.pdf:/srv/in
The user and host belong with the remote path, not the file name.
ssh report.pdf ana@fs1:/srv/in
ssh opens a login and does not copy files.
scp report.pdf fs1@ana:/srv/in
The user comes before the @ sign and the host after.

q.q: Which file holds the password hashes and is readable only by root?
o: /etc/shadow
Right. Hashes were moved out of /etc/passwd into the more tightly locked /etc/shadow.
/etc/passwd
This lists accounts and can be read by every user.
/etc/group
This lists groups and their members.
/etc/skel
This holds the starter files given to new users.

q.q: Which command creates the account lee and also makes the home folder?
o: sudo passwd lee
passwd sets a password for an account that already exists.
sudo useradd -m lee
Right. useradd adds the account, and -m creates the home folder.
sudo groupadd -m lee
groupadd only creates a group and has no -m option.
id lee
id shows information about an existing account.

q.q: Where do the default files copied into a new user's home folder come from?
o: /etc/shadow
This stores password hashes.
/var/tmp
This holds temporary files kept across reboots.
/etc/skel
Right. The skeleton folder holds starter files like .bashrc.
/usr/share/doc
This holds package documentation.

q.q: Which command lists recent logins, including sessions that already ended?
o: users
users prints only the names of people logged in now.
whoami
whoami prints only your own user name.
who
who lists only users who are logged in now.
last
Right. last reads the login history and lists past and current sessions.

q.q: A file shows -rwxr-x--- in ls -l. Who may execute it?
o: The owner and members of the file's group
Right. The owner has rwx and the group has r-x. Others have no permissions.
Only the owner
The group part also contains an x.
Everyone on the system
Others have no permission at all.
Nobody, because it is not a script
Execute permission is separate from what the file contains.

q.q: Which command gives the owner read and write, the group read only, and others nothing?
o: chmod 604 notes.txt
This gives the group nothing and others read.
chmod 460 notes.txt
This gives the owner read only and the group read and write.
chmod 750 notes.txt
This gives the owner full rights, which adds execute.
chmod 640 notes.txt
Right. 6 is read plus write, 4 is read, and 0 is nothing.

q.q: Which command adds the execute permission for the owner of run.sh only?
o: chmod o+x run.sh
o is for others, which means everyone else.
chmod u+x run.sh
Right. u means user (the owner), and +x adds execute.
chmod a-x run.sh
a-x would remove execute for all.
chmod g+x run.sh
g is for the group.

q.q: Which command makes bob the owner and staff the group of data.csv?
o: chown staff:bob data.csv
This swaps them, making staff the owner and bob the group.
chmod bob:staff data.csv
chmod changes permission bits and does not accept a user:group.
chown bob:staff data.csv
Right. chown takes owner:group, in that order.
chgrp bob staff
This would set the group bob on a file named staff.

q.q: The /tmp folder shows drwxrwxrwt. What does the final t mean?
o: The folder holds only temporary text files
The t is a permission flag, not about file type.
Only root may write in the folder
Everyone can write there, as the rwx for others shows.
The folder is a symbolic link
A link would start with an l in the first column.
The sticky bit, so users can only delete their own files there
Right. With the sticky bit set, only the file's owner (or root) can delete or rename it, even though everyone can write in the folder.

q.q: Which command creates a symbolic link named latest that points to /data/v2?
o: ln -s /data/v2 latest
Right. ln -s takes the target first and the link name second.
ln -s latest /data/v2
This reverses the two names.
ln /data/v2 latest
Without -s this makes a hard link, and it fails for folders.
mv /data/v2 latest
This moves the folder and does not create a link.
